title: Borrow, then personalize
text:
The question
When you look at a picture, your brain answers with a pattern. We can record it with EEG (sensors on the head) or with fMRI (a scanner). An encoding model takes the image and predicts this pattern.
A good model for one person needs many hours of their recordings. A new person usually gives much less, maybe a few hundred labelled images. But we already have models of many other people. So my question was simple:

If I have only a few hundred images from a new person, what is the best way to use them, when models of other people already exist?

I did this work on free Kaggle notebooks. I had no GPU of my own, so every idea had to be cheap enough to run there.

title: Borrow, then personalize
section: First, what the data looks like
text:
First, what the data looks like
Everything later in this post is easier if you know what one piece of data is. So let me show it first.
In all five datasets the setup is similar. A person sits and looks at many photos of objects and scenes, one after another, while a machine records their brain. Each photo gives one brain response. One photo together with this person’s response to it is what I call a labelled image. A model learns from these pairs.

  🖼️1. A photo
    A cat, a banana, a street… Thousands of different photos, some of them shown many times.
  →
  🧠2. A recording
    EEG: a cap of sensors on the head measures fast electrical signals.
    fMRI: a scanner measures slow changes of blood flow in small spots of the brain.
  →
  📈3. A response
    EEG: 17 sensors at the back of the head, 100 time points in one second.
    fMRI: one number for each of tens of thousands of brain spots.

These are the five datasets I used. Three are EEG and two are fMRI. The first number on each card is how many people I tested as “new people”.

  THINGS-EEG1EEG · lab
    24 new people64-sensor lab capPhotos flash quickly; training photos recorded once
    Up to about 22,000 labelled images per person
  THINGS-EEG2EEG · lab
    10 people64-sensor lab capTraining photos shown 4 times, test photos 80 times
    Up to 16,540 labelled images per person
  Alljoined-1.6MEEG · consumer
    16 people32-sensor consumer headset, cheaper and noisierSame photo set as THINGS-EEG2
  NSDfMRI · 7 tesla
    8 peopleVery strong scanner, very clean dataUp to 3 repeats per photo, averaged
    About 8,000 to 9,000 labelled images per person
  NODfMRI · 3 tesla
    21 new peopleCommon hospital-strength scannerEach photo recorded only once
    800 labelled images per person

I can’t show the real photos here, because their licences don’t allow it. But one dataset, THINGS-EEG2, shares its recordings openly, so Figure 1, Figure 2 and Figure 3 use real EEG. I took the test part of the data (200 photos, each shown 80 times to each of the 10 people) and made small averages from it on Kaggle.
A real response. Figure 1 shows the signal of one sensor at the back of the head (Oz, above the visual cortex) for five photos. Time 0 is the moment the photo appears. In this dataset the photos come very fast, a new one every 200 ms, so the line is never flat: you also see the waves of the photos before and after, and that makes the regular ripple. The response to this photo is where the five coloured lines split apart, most clearly in the grey band, 100 to 200 ms. That early response is what I scored in the EEG tests. Pick another person from the menu: the general shape stays, but the details move.




                                                


Figure 1: Real EEG from THINGS-EEG2 (Gifford et al., 2022, CC-BY 4.0), sensor Oz. Each coloured line is the average over the 80 times one photo was shown. Dashed grey: the average over all 200 test photos. The data are noise-normalised per person, so the scale has no unit.




One photo, 80 times. The five coloured lines in Figure 1 are averages over 80 recordings each. A single recording is very noisy. In Figure 2 each thin grey line is one of the 80 times the same person saw the same cat photo, and the thick green line is their average. You can almost not see the response in a single line, but the average shows it clearly. Keep this in mind: later it explains why the method works on some datasets and not on others.




                                                


Figure 2: Real EEG from THINGS-EEG2, sensor Oz, the cat photo. Thin lines: the 80 single recordings of one person. Thick line: their average.




Are two people similar? This is the key question for the whole project. For each person I split the 80 repeats into two halves of 40, and asked (in Figure 3) how similar the patterns over all 200 photos are: between the two halves of the same person, and between two different people. 1 means the same pattern, 0 means no relation.




                                                


Figure 3: Real EEG from THINGS-EEG2. Similarity (correlation) of the responses to the 200 test photos, all 17 sensors and time points, after removing each half’s average response. Row: first half of the repeats; column: second half. The diagonal compares a person with themself. Hover a cell to see its value.




In Figure 3, the squares on the diagonal are darker than the rest. On average, two halves of the same person are similar at 0.39, and two different people at 0.15. This is not zero: people respond to the same photos in a similar way. That is why borrowing from other people works at all. But it is clearly lower than the same person: each person also has their own part. That is the part a personal map should learn.
The idea in one (made-up) picture. Figure 4 is not real data. It is a small made-up example of a brain map, to show the idea of the project before the real results. Each person’s response is a shared part, plus a personal part, plus noise. If you average many other people, their personal parts cancel out and the shared part stays: this is borrowing. What is left between borrowing and the person is what the personal map must learn from that person’s few labelled images. Pick a person from the menu above Figure 4.




                                                


Figure 4: Made-up example, not real data: a grid of ‘brain spots’ responding to one photo. Left: one person’s response. Middle: the average of the four other people (borrowing). Right: the difference between them, which the personal map has to learn.




With this picture in mind, the rest of the post is the story of how I found that borrowing is a strong start, and that a small personal map on top of it helps when the person’s labelled images are clean enough.

title: Borrow, then personalize
text:
The path, in one picture

IdeaOne big shared network for all people, with a small part for each person.
Reproduce firstA published EEG model and its baselines, number by number.
Looks goodThe shared network wins on the ten people I built it with.
The real testWritten down first, run once on 24 new people. It loses to a simple average.
BorrowAverage the models of other people. No labels needed.
PersonalizeA small linear map on top, learned from a few hundred images.
Test againSecond lab EEG, consumer EEG, 7-tesla fMRI, single-trial 3-tesla fMRI.
WhyThe map needs room to improve and clean labels.

title: Borrow, then personalize
section: Where I started: a big shared network
text:
Where I started: a big shared network
At the start I followed the trend in the field. Many recent papers train one network on many people and add a small part for each person. My plan was the same: a shared core for everyone, a small adapter for each new person, and later some extra ideas on top, like contrastive training across people.
Before building anything, I reproduced a published EEG encoding model and its baselines, and checked that my numbers matched the paper. This step was slow and boring, but later it saved me. Every new idea was compared with baselines that I knew were correct.
On THINGS-EEG2 (ten people) the shared network looked good. With 250 or 500 images from a new person it beat the baselines. I was happy. But there was a problem: I had used these same ten people while building the model. A model can look good on the people it was tuned on.

title: Borrow, then personalize
section: The test that changed the project
text:
The test that changed the project
So I wrote the test down before running it. In a protocol, committed to git, I fixed the model, the people, the score, the margin a gain must clear, and the decision rule. Then I ran it once, on 24 people of a second EEG dataset (THINGS-EEG1) that no model had seen.
The shared network beat a model trained only on the person’s own few hundred images. But it lost to something much simpler: just average the predictions of the models of other people. I call this borrowing. The test said “rejected”, and I kept that result.
In Figure 5, use the menu above the chart to switch between the two comparisons. Each line is one person; coloured lines go up, grey lines go down. Hover a point to see the person.




                                                


Figure 5: THINGS-EEG1, 24 new people. Encoding accuracy (correlation, 100 to 200 ms after the image). First choice: each person’s own model from 250 to 500 images against borrowing. Second choice: borrowing against the shared network, in the first test.




In Figure 5, borrowing was better than the person’s own model for 22 of 24 people. The shared network was below borrowing for 18 of 24.
This was the most important moment of the project. I had spent a lot of time on the big network, and a plain average of other people beat it, on people it had never seen. If I had not written the test first, I could have searched for some setting where the network wins, and I would have believed it.

title: Borrow, then personalize
text:
Borrow, then personalize
So I changed the direction. If borrowing is such a strong start, the new person’s few hundred images should not build a model from zero. They should correct the borrowed prediction.
The correction is small on purpose. It is a regularised linear map that mixes the borrowed prediction across EEG sensors (or fMRI vertices) in the way this one person needs. I call it the personal map. Two steps:

Borrow. Average the predictions of encoders trained on other people. No labels of the new person needed.
Personalize. Fit the small map from the new person’s labelled images, on top of that average.

Then I did the same as before: protocol first, one run, a fixed margin. On the 24 THINGS-EEG1 people the map improved on borrowing for 23 of them, in the early visual response. To be honest about it: this follow-up used the same 24 people as the first test, and I wrote it after I saw the first result.

title: Borrow, then personalize
section: Does it hold on other data?
text:
Does it hold on other data?
One dataset is not enough. So I wrote new protocols and tested the same idea on four more datasets: a second lab EEG dataset, a consumer EEG headset, 7-tesla fMRI and single-trial 3-tesla fMRI. Each test was run once.
In Figure 6 every dot is one person. Above zero means the map was better than borrowing for that person. The red dashed line is the margin that the protocol said a gain must clear. Hover a dot for the person, or a diamond for the mean and its interval.




                                                


Figure 6: The personal map minus borrowing, in every test that was written down before scoring. Dots: people. Diamonds and bars: the mean and the interval the decision used. Red dashed: the margin. Filled diamond: the interval is fully on one side of the margin; empty: it is not.




What Figure 6 says, in short:

Lab EEG (THINGS-EEG1 and THINGS-EEG2): the map helped, for almost every person. On THINGS-EEG2 it cleared the margin over borrowing, but not over every other method in that test, so that test as a whole did not pass. THINGS-EEG2’s people were also the ones I used to build the baselines, so it is the weaker of the two.
Consumer EEG (Alljoined, 16 people): the gain went the same way, for 12 of 16 people, but did not clear the margin. The answer here is “not sure”, and I report it like that.
7-tesla fMRI (NSD, 8 people): the map helped every person. Encoding accuracy went up by about a fifth.
Single-trial 3-tesla fMRI (NOD, 21 people): no gain. And this was the result I had predicted in the protocol, before the test. The next section says why.

title: Borrow, then personalize
section: Why it works sometimes and not always
text:
Why it works sometimes and not always
The pattern became clear from the development work. The map can only fix what borrowing leaves on the table. It needs two things:

Room. If borrowing is already close to the best that the noisy data allows, there is nothing left to gain.
Clean labels. The map learns from the new person’s responses. If each response is very noisy, the map learns noise.

NOD records each image only once, on a 3-tesla scanner, so its labels are very noisy. That is why I predicted no gain there, and the test agreed.
The clean-label part I could check directly on THINGS-EEG2, where each image was shown several times. I trained the map on labels that averaged 1, 2 or 4 repetitions, and kept everything else the same. In Figure 7, use the menu above the chart to switch between two kinds of map and two label budgets.




                                                


Figure 7: THINGS-EEG2 (development analysis). Gain of the map over borrowing when each labelled response is the average of 1, 2 or 4 repetitions. Thin lines: people. Thick grey line: the mean.




Figure 7 shows that with cleaner labels the gain grows, for the same people and the same number of images. So the few hundred images of a new person are worth more when each one is recorded well.

title: Borrow, then personalize
section: Encoding is not the same as identifying
text:
Encoding is not the same as identifying
In fMRI I also looked at a second task: given a brain response, which of 200 images was the person looking at? Here I found something I did not expect. The best model for predicting the response is not always the best model for picking the image. In the main fMRI test, the map combined with the person’s own model picked the right image 7.4 points more often than borrowing.
Figure 8 follows the same people while they give more and more labelled images, up to their whole recording. It uses stronger image features (DINOv2) than the main test, so all numbers are higher. Click a name in the legend to hide or show it. Each thin line is one person.




                                                


Figure 8: NSD, 8 people (development analysis, DINOv2 features). Identification among 200 images by the number of labelled images of the new person. Thin lines: people. Thick lines: the mean. Dashed: borrowing, which uses no labels.




In Figure 8, with 500 images the map on borrowing is far ahead of the person’s own model. With more images the own model catches up, but even with the whole recording the map stays a little ahead, and adding the own model to it helps a bit more. Borrowing matters most when you have little data from the person, and it does not hurt when you have a lot.

title: Borrow, then personalize
text:
What I take from it

Write the test before you run it. My first idea failed its test. Without the protocol I would have kept the wrong story.
Try the simple thing first. A plain average of other people was stronger than the network I spent so long on.
Reproduce before you improve. Correct baselines made every later comparison clear.
Small and cheap can be enough. All of this ran on free Kaggle notebooks. The final method is a few lines of linear algebra.
Say “not sure” when the data says “not sure”. The consumer EEG result is inconclusive, and it stays like that.

title: Borrow, then personalize
text:
Limits
The EEG gains are small, a few hundredths in correlation. Each confirmation used one dataset. Some tests reused people that I had seen before (the THINGS-EEG1 follow-ups and the THINGS-EEG2 replication), and I say this in each place. The parts about room, label noise and identification are development analyses, not prespecified tests.

title: Borrow, then personalize
text:
Where to look
Everything is on GitHub: the code, the protocols of every test, the commit that holds each protocol before its run, and the result tables behind every figure. The charts on this page are built from those tables with a short script (data/prepare_data.py in this post’s source folder). The real EEG examples come from the openly shared THINGS-EEG2 recordings (Gifford et al., 2022, CC-BY 4.0), averaged by a small Kaggle script (data/kaggle_eeg_examples/ in the same folder).
